screens.title: Physical Backups and WAL Archiving
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will meet the fundamental pieces of PostgreSQL disaster recovery: file-system level physical backups and the Write‑Ahead Log, often called WAL. Physical backups are fast binary snapshots of PGDATA, while WAL records every change so the server can replay history after a crash. Together they let you restore a cluster not just to the moment of the base backup but to any later point in time, provided the necessary WAL files were archived. You will learn the role of archive_mode and archive_command in postgresql. conf, how WAL segment files live in pg_wal, and why a broken archive command can halt your database if not fixed. A concrete example will walk you through creating an archive directory, tuning the configuration, generating WAL activity, and checking that segments appear in the archive. Along the way we’ll highlight common mistakes, like archiving into PGDATA or using an unreliable copy command, and explain safe practices such as testing permissions and avoiding overwrites. By the end you should be able to explain why physical backups plus continuous WAL archiving are the backbone of low‑RPO recovery and what checks to run to keep that chain intact.

screens.title: What is a Physical Backup?
screens.narratorSegment: A physical backup is a file‑system level copy of the PostgreSQL data directory, often referred to as PGDATA. It copies database files, configuration, and the pg_wal directory content as binary files — not S Q L statements. Because it captures the exact on‑disk format, it's faster for large datasets and restores are generally quicker than rebuilding data from logical S Q L exports. A critical point is consistency: copying PGDATA while the server is running can produce a corrupt backup because files are changing. To avoid that, either stop the server to capture a cold backup or use an atomic backup tool designed for running systems. The chapter highlights pg_basebackup as the safe utility for creating consistent base backups while the server runs; we will cover the tool itself in the next chapter. Example: imagine copying a running database's files while a table is being rewritten; without WAL replay or a proper backup process, those files might represent mismatched states. A common misconception is to assume file copy equals safe backup; in PostgreSQL the file-state must be consistent or accompanied by WAL segments to be usable. Key takeaway: physical backups are fast and necessary for large systems, but they must be produced in a way that preserves on-disk consistency.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Physical backups are binary copies of PGDATA; they must be consistent or paired with WAL to be useful.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › What is a Physical Backup?
Physical backup explained
A binary snapshot of PGDATA including data files, configuration, and WAL files.
Why use physical backups?
Faster for large volumes and simpler to restore because files are copied directly.
Consistency requirement
Cold stop or a backup tool is required; arbitrary copies while running risk corruption.
Common misconception
Copying files equals safe backup — not true unless files are consistent or WAL is available for replay.
Key Takeaway

Physical backups are binary and fast, but must be created consistently or combined with WAL files to be recoverable.

Concrete example
You want to back up a large production cluster. A logical dump would take too long. Instead, you make a physical base backup and then archive WALs so you can restore quickly and replay recent changes.
Analogy
Think of the base backup as a high-resolution photo and the WAL archive as the continuous video footage that follows it.
Check your understanding
  • Can you explain why a running file copy can corrupt a backup?
  • When would you prefer a physical backup over a logical dump?

screens.title: Physical vs Logical Backups
screens.narratorSegment: PostgreSQL supports both logical and physical backups, and each has strengths. Logical backups export S Q L statements or data rows and are portable across PostgreSQL versions or architectures. They are flexible for extracting specific tables but are slower and less suitable for very large datasets. Physical backups are binary copies of PGDATA and restore faster for large clusters. They require the same major PostgreSQL version and a compatible file layout. A concrete decision example: for migrating a single table between versions, a logical dump is convenient. For restoring an entire multi-terabyte cluster after disk failure, a physical base backup plus WAL replay is the practical choice. A common misconception is that physical backups make WAL unnecessary — they do not. A base backup alone restores the snapshot moment, but archived WAL files are required to reach any point after that snapshot. Conversely, relying only on WAL without a base backup is impossible because WAL files replay changes but need a starting consistent image. The core trade-off is speed and completeness versus portability and flexibility. Physical vs Logical Backups means logical = portable and flexible; physical = fast for full restores and necessary for low rpo when paired with wal archives.. In practical terms, when to use each and the trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Logical = portable and flexible; Physical = fast for full restores and necessary for low RPO when paired with WAL archives.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Physical vs Logical
Physical backups
  • Binary copy of PGDATA; fast to take and restore for large datasets.
  • Requires compatible on-disk layout and often same PostgreSQL major version.
  • Must be combined with WAL archives to recover beyond the snapshot.
When to choose

Choose physical for whole-cluster, large-scale recovery and low RPO when you can manage WAL archiving.

Logical backups
  • Exported SQL or data; portable and useful for partial restores or migrations.
  • Can be slower and heavy for very large databases.
  • Not sufficient for low-RPO continuous recovery alone.
Example decision
Migrate one table between versions: logical. Recover entire multi-terabyte cluster quickly: physical plus WAL.

screens.title: Write‑Ahead Log (WAL) Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: Write‑Ahead Logging is a fundamental mechanism that ensures data integrity in PostgreSQL. WAL records every change before that change is applied to the data files. This ordering guarantees that, after a crash, PostgreSQL can replay WAL records to bring data files to a consistent state that includes committed transactions. The WAL files are append-only segment files stored in the pg_wal directory within PGDATA and have names like a long hexadecimal sequence. A concrete example: when you insert a row, PostgreSQL writes the change to WAL first; only then does it modify the table file. If the server crashes mid-write, replaying the WAL ensures the committed insert is restored or partially applied operations are rolled back to a consistent state. A common misconception is that WAL is only for replication; in fact WAL is central to local crash recovery as well. Key operational point: WAL enables low RPO when archived because those archived segments contain every committed change after a base backup. Reflect: how would you detect that WAL replay happened successfully during a recovery? Write‑Ahead Log (WAL) Fundamentals means wal records every change before data files are updated, enabling replay-based crash recovery and pitr.. In practical terms, why wal exists and how it guarantees crash recovery. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: WAL in one line
keyIdea.text: WAL records every change before data files are updated, enabling replay-based crash recovery and PITR.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › WAL Fundamentals
What WAL records
  • Every change before the change is applied to on-disk data files.
  • Stored as segment files in pg_wal with sequential names.
  • Used for crash recovery and to reach a point after a base backup.
Concrete example
An INSERT writes WAL records first; on crash, WAL replay restores the committed insert even if data files were not synced.
Misconception check
WAL is not only for replication; it is essential for crash recovery on the same server and for enabling PITR when archived properly.
Why this matters
Because WAL contains the authoritative sequence of changes, keeping it archived ensures you can restore up to a precise moment.
Key Takeaway

WAL is the change log that makes safe recovery and fine‑grained restore possible.

screens.title: Where WAL Lives: pg_wal and Segment Files
screens.narratorSegment: WAL segments are stored inside the pg_wal subdirectory within PGDATA. Each completed segment is a file with a long hexadecimal-style name that encodes timeline and position. These segment files are created as the system generates WAL activity; once a segment is completed it can be archived if archiving is enabled. Operationally, pg_wal is limited in space — if archiving fails and segments cannot be removed, pg_wal grows and can eventually fill storage, causing the server to halt writes. That’s why a robust archive_command and external archive space are essential. A concrete example: if your archive_command fails repeatedly, the server will keep the unarchived segments in pg_wal and block cleanup. Check pg_wal size and use monitoring to alert when it grows unexpectedly. A common mistake is placing the archive target inside PGDATA — this can create circular dependencies or even be blocked by server protections. Key point: pg_wal holds active WAL segments; archives live elsewhere and must be reliable to prevent backlog in pg_wal. Where WAL Lives: pg_wal and Segment Files means pg_wal stores active wal segment files; reliable archiving prevents pg_wal from filling and stopping database operations.. In practical terms, segment naming, storage, and capacity considerations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: pg_wal stores active WAL segment files; reliable archiving prevents pg_wal from filling and stopping database operations.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › pg_wal & Segments
pg_wal contents
Active WAL segment files created as the server runs. Completed segments are candidates for archiving.
Segment naming
Files are named by timeline and position — long hex sequences that identify order.
Capacity risk
If archiving fails, pg_wal retains segments and can fill disk, halting the server eventually.
Operational checks
  • Monitor pg_wal directory size and file count.
  • Review PostgreSQL logs for archive_command failures.
  • Ensure archive target has adequate free space and permissions.
Common mistake
Archiving into a directory inside PGDATA can be blocked or cause confusing behavior; always use external storage.
Key Takeaway

Keep pg_wal small by reliably archiving completed segments to an external, permissioned store.

screens.title: archive_mode: enabling WAL archiving
screens.narratorSegment: archive_mode is the postgresql. conf parameter that enables WAL archiving. It accepts values such as off, on, and always. For most PITR setups you set it to on so completed WAL segments are sent to your archive location. The chapter notes that always is used for standby systems in streaming replication so they keep archiving even when promoted in certain scenarios. Importantly, changing archive_mode requires a server restart because it controls a core background behavior. A concrete example: you edit postgresql. conf to set archive_mode to on, restart the server, then observe that completed WAL segments are now handed to archive_command for copying. A common misconception is to expect archive_mode changes to take effect with a reload — they do not. Operationally, plan restarts during maintenance windows and verify archive entries after restart. Finally, archive_mode is only one half of the setup; archive_command must be present and reliable for archiving to work. archive_mode: enabling WAL archiving means set archive_mode to on for pitr; changes require a full server restart to take effect.. In practical terms, how archive_mode controls archiving behavior and restart requirements. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Set archive_mode to on for PITR; changes require a full server restart to take effect.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › archive_mode
What archive_mode does
Turns WAL archiving on or off. Use on for PITR setups.
Important note
Changing archive_mode requires a full server restart to take effect.
Example postgresql.conf snippet
# postgresql.conf wal_level = replica archive_mode = on # After restart, completed WAL segments will be handed to archive_command for copying
After editing, restart PostgreSQL and confirm archive pieces appear in the archive target directory.

screens.title: archive_command: writing a robust command
screens.narratorSegment: archive_command is the shell command PostgreSQL runs to copy each completed WAL segment to your archive location. The command receives two placeholders: the full path of the WAL file and the filename. It must return zero on success and non‑zero on failure. The chapter gives an example that includes a test to avoid overwriting: running a shell test to check if the destination file exists and only copying if it does not. A robust command handles transient errors, ensures correct file ownership, and writes to external storage with sufficient capacity. A concrete common failure mode: a simple copy to a path inside PGDATA or a non‑writable directory. If the archive_command fails, PostgreSQL will repeatedly try to archive the same segment, causing pg_wal to fill. Always test your archive_command as the postgres user and check logs for failures. Finally, if you use cloud storage, wrap reliable client tools in the command and verify exit codes carefully. archive_command: writing a robust command means a shell command that must copy wal files reliably and return success; failures lead to repeated retries and possible disk fill.. In practical terms, syntax, arguments, and common failure modes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: archive_command
keyIdea.text: A shell command that must copy WAL files reliably and return success; failures lead to repeated retries and possible disk fill.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › archive_command
Principles of a good archive_command
  • Return zero only on successful copy.
  • Avoid overwriting existing files unless intended.
  • Run as the postgres OS user with correct permissions.
Warning

A failing archive_command will cause PostgreSQL to retry indefinitely and can fill pg_wal.

Example safe command
# postgresql.conf example archive_command = 'test ! -f /mnt/pg_wal_archive/%f && cp %p /mnt/pg_wal_archive/%f' # Ensures we don't overwrite an existing archived WAL file.
Test this command manually as the postgres user and verify exit codes. For cloud targets, prefer client tools that return proper exit codes.

screens.title: How WAL Archiving Works
screens.narratorSegment: WAL archiving is a simple, repeatable process: PostgreSQL completes a WAL segment, invokes archive_command with the segment path and filename, and expects the command to copy the segment to the archive location and exit successfully. If the command succeeds, PostgreSQL marks that segment as archived and may remove or reuse it later. If it fails, PostgreSQL keeps the segment and retries; repeated failures cause pg_wal to accumulate files. A concrete lifecycle example: as you run transactions, segments fill and rotate. Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › WAL Archiving Flow
Steps
  1. Transaction writes are recorded in WAL segments.
  2. When a segment is complete, PostgreSQL runs archive_command with %p and %f.
  3. If the command succeeds (exit 0), the segment is archived; if not, PostgreSQL retries.
Operational tip
Monitor both archive directory contents and database logs for archive_command failures to avoid pg_wal backlogs.
Concrete scenario
During heavy DML, multiple segments complete quickly. A robust archive_command copies them to external storage; if the external network is slow, archive_command must still indicate failure clearly so the DBA can intervene before disk fills.
Key Takeaway

Archiving is a lifecycle: complete segment → copy → confirm success. Reliability and monitoring keep the pipeline healthy.

screens.title: PITR Workflow: Base Backup + WAL Replay
screens.narratorSegment: Point‑in‑Time Recovery uses a base backup as the starting image and then replays archived WAL segments to reach a target moment or transaction. The workflow is straightforward: restore the most recent base backup into a new data directory, configure recovery settings pointing at your archive store, and instruct PostgreSQL to replay archived WAL segments. You can stop replay at a timestamp, transaction ID, or named restore point. A concrete example: after restoring a base backup from yesterday, you replay archived WALs until just before an accidental drop table occurred mid‑afternoon. Misconceptions arise when people expect PITR to work without a proper set of WAL archives; replay is impossible without the WAL files generated since the base backup. Operationally, ensure your archive sequence is continuous and that no segments are missing. Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Hands-on Activity
Steps to perform

  2. Edit postgresql.conf: set wal_level, archive_mode, and archive_command.

Manual test tip
Run your archive_command as the postgres user to confirm it returns zero and copies the file where expected.
Commands (illustrative)
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/pg_wal_archive sudo chown -R postgres:postgres /mnt/pg_wal_archive # Edit postgresql.conf: # wal_level = replica # archive_mode = on # archive_command = 'test ! -f /mnt/pg_wal_archive/%f && cp %p /mnt/pg_wal_archive/%f' sudo systemctl restart postgresql@12-main # Generate activity with psql and then: ls -l /mnt/pg_wal_archive
If no WAL files appear, check PostgreSQL logs for archive_command errors and confirm path and permissions.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and How to Monitor Archiving
screens.narratorSegment: Several recurring mistakes can break WAL archiving. One is archiving into a directory that resides inside PGDATA — this risks circular behavior and is often blocked. Another is using an archive_command that overwrites files or returns success incorrectly. Also, insufficient space or wrong permissions on the archive target will cause failures. The chapter points out the severe consequence: PostgreSQL will keep retrying a failed archive_command, retaining segments in pg_wal and eventually preventing further progress. Monitoring mitigates these issues: track pg_wal size and file count, monitor archive directory growth, and alert on archive_command errors in PostgreSQL logs. A practical verification habit is to run the archive_command manually as the postgres user to confirm exit codes and file placement. Finally, schedule regular checks of your recovery chain — ensure base backups are recent and that WAL archives cover the interval since the last base backup. The closing question: what alert thresholds would you set to detect a growing pg_wal before it causes problems? fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will meet the fundamental pieces of PostgreSQL disaster recovery: file-system level physical backups and the Write‑Ahead Log, often called WAL. Physical backups are fast binary snapshots of PGDATA, while WAL records every change so the server can replay history after a crash. Together they let you restore a cluster not just to the moment of the base backup but to any later point in time, provided the necessary WAL files were archived. You will learn the role of archive_mode and archive_command in postgresql. conf, how WAL segment files live in pg_wal, and why a broken archive command can halt your database if not fixed. A concrete example will walk you through creating an archive directory, tuning the configuration, generating WAL activity, and checking that segments appear in the archive. Along the way we’ll highlight common mistakes, like archiving into PGDATA or using an unreliable copy command, and explain safe practices such as testing permissions and avoiding overwrites. By the end you should be able to explain why physical backups plus continuous WAL archiving are the backbone of low‑RPO recovery and what checks to run to keep that chain intact.

These objectives orient your learning and map to the chapter content. First, you will be able to explain what a physical backup is and how it maps to the PGDATA directory. This includes why copying files blindly while a server runs can corrupt a backup. Second, you will understand Write‑Ahead Log fundamentals: why WAL records each change before it is applied and how that supports crash recovery. Third, you will learn how WAL archiving works, why continuous archiving is necessary for Point‑in‑Time Recovery, and how WAL segments are stored and named. Finally on this screen you will identify the important postgresql. conf parameters for archiving. Each objective includes a short practice cue so you can confirm competency by locating the relevant files or lines in your configuration. Together these skills let you design and verify a reliable base‑backup plus WAL archive workflow that meets low Recovery Point Objectives.

On this second objectives slide you will gain applied skills. First, you will learn to plan and verify an archive location that is external to PGDATA with correct ownership and space. Second, you will practice forming a safe archive_command that returns success codes and avoids overwriting files, and you will understand the consequences of a failing command. Third, you’ll learn the PITR principle: combine a recent base backup with all subsequent archived WAL segments to restore to any point in time. Finally, you will be able to perform basic checks: list archived WAL segment files and read PostgreSQL logs for archive_command errors. Each objective is paired with a small mnemonic to help you remember the verification steps and a milestone prompt to mark competency when you can demonstrate an archive listing and a successful archive_command run.

A physical backup is a file‑system level copy of the PostgreSQL data directory, often referred to as PGDATA. It copies database files, configuration, and the pg_wal directory content as binary files — not S Q L statements. Because it captures the exact on‑disk format, it's faster for large datasets and restores are generally quicker than rebuilding data from logical S Q L exports. A critical point is consistency: copying PGDATA while the server is running can produce a corrupt backup because files are changing. To avoid that, either stop the server to capture a cold backup or use an atomic backup tool designed for running systems. The chapter highlights pg_basebackup as the safe utility for creating consistent base backups while the server runs; we will cover the tool itself in the next chapter. Example: imagine copying a running database's files while a table is being rewritten; without WAL replay or a proper backup process, those files might represent mismatched states. A common misconception is to assume file copy equals safe backup; in PostgreSQL the file-state must be consistent or accompanied by WAL segments to be usable. Key takeaway: physical backups are fast and necessary for large systems, but they must be produced in a way that preserves on-disk consistency.

PostgreSQL supports both logical and physical backups, and each has strengths. Logical backups export S Q L statements or data rows and are portable across PostgreSQL versions or architectures. They are flexible for extracting specific tables but are slower and less suitable for very large datasets. Physical backups are binary copies of PGDATA and restore faster for large clusters. They require the same major PostgreSQL version and a compatible file layout. A concrete decision example: for migrating a single table between versions, a logical dump is convenient. For restoring an entire multi-terabyte cluster after disk failure, a physical base backup plus WAL replay is the practical choice. A common misconception is that physical backups make WAL unnecessary — they do not. A base backup alone restores the snapshot moment, but archived WAL files are required to reach any point after that snapshot. Conversely, relying only on WAL without a base backup is impossible because WAL files replay changes but need a starting consistent image. The core trade-off is speed and completeness versus portability and flexibility. Physical vs Logical Backups means logical = portable and flexible; physical = fast for full restores and necessary for low rpo when paired with wal archives.. In practical terms, when to use each and the trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Write‑Ahead Logging is a fundamental mechanism that ensures data integrity in PostgreSQL. WAL records every change before that change is applied to the data files. This ordering guarantees that, after a crash, PostgreSQL can replay WAL records to bring data files to a consistent state that includes committed transactions. The WAL files are append-only segment files stored in the pg_wal directory within PGDATA and have names like a long hexadecimal sequence. A concrete example: when you insert a row, PostgreSQL writes the change to WAL first; only then does it modify the table file. If the server crashes mid-write, replaying the WAL ensures the committed insert is restored or partially applied operations are rolled back to a consistent state. A common misconception is that WAL is only for replication; in fact WAL is central to local crash recovery as well. Key operational point: WAL enables low RPO when archived because those archived segments contain every committed change after a base backup. WAL segments are stored inside the pg_wal subdirectory within PGDATA. Each completed segment is a file with a long hexadecimal-style name that encodes timeline and position. These segment files are created as the system generates WAL activity; once a segment is completed it can be archived if archiving is enabled. Point‑in‑Time Recovery uses a base backup as the starting image and then replays archived WAL segments to reach a target moment or transaction. The workflow is straightforward: restore the most recent base backup into a new data directory, configure recovery settings pointing at your archive store, and instruct PostgreSQL to replay archived WAL segments. Several recurring mistakes can break WAL archiving. One is archiving into a directory that resides inside PGDATA — this risks circular behavior and is often blocked. Another is using an archive_command that overwrites files or returns success incorrectly. Also, insufficient space or wrong permissions on the archive target will cause failures. The chapter points out the severe consequence: PostgreSQL will keep retrying a failed archive_command, retaining segments in pg_wal and eventually preventing further progress. Monitoring mitigates these issues: track pg_wal size and file count, monitor archive directory growth, and alert on archive_command errors in PostgreSQL logs. A practical verification habit is to run the archive_command manually as the postgres user to confirm exit codes and file placement. These three core concepts capture the chapter's essentials. First, a physical backup is a binary copy of the PGDATA directory; it gives a fast, exact snapshot but must be consistent. Second, the Write‑Ahead Log records every change before data files are updated; WAL enables crash recovery and forms the change stream for PITR. Third, WAL archiving uses archive_mode and archive_command to copy completed WAL segments to an external store; archive reliability is essential because failures cause retries and can fill pg_wal. Keep in mind that PITR requires both a base backup and the sequence of archived WAL files generated after that backup. Monitoring pg_wal and the archive location, testing archive_command manually, and avoiding archiving into PGDATA are practical habits that keep your recovery chain intact. Three operational reminders summarize safe behavior. First, never archive WAL into PGDATA — choose an external location owned by postgres with enough space. Third, monitor pg_wal size and archived file listings; set alerts so you detect archiving failures before they cause a disk‑full halt.
